newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE - Oil a mixed blessing in Venezuela delta.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oil a mixed blessing in Venezuela delta.

text.p: At six in the morning on a secluded river bank in the heart of Venezuela's Orinoco delta, a Warao Indian rests near his dugout canoe after a hard night's harpoon fishing.

Suddenly the silence is broken by a deafening roar as a man in a bright red lifejacket and sunglasses zooms past on a small hovercraft. Not far away, helicopters circle above an oil rig the size of a skyscraper.
The Orinoco delta, Venezuela's most remote and poorest eastern state, is experiencing change at a dizzying pace.

The scene is reminiscent of oil booms the world over as doctors, researchers, engineers, geologists and bureaucrats pour into the region bringing cash, crime and social upheaval. But here it is happening in one of the world's hubs of biodiversity inhabited by a marginalized Indian tribe.

"What's happening in the delta is the meeting of two worlds, it's like the discovery of America is happening again," said John Dinan, project manager for the Zumaque Foundation, commissioned by oil companies to study the Warao.

Big oil came to the delta once before, in the 1920s. But when the oil dried up the companies upped sticks, leaving towns with pollution but no jobs. This time, under Venezuela's oil industry liberalisation, or apertura, three foreign oil consortia won contracts in the delta, British Petroleum, Amoco and a group comprising Louisiana Land, Norcen and Benton.
Environmental groups and politicians have called for an end to their activities, saying they are polluting the water and changing the Warao way of life.
LACKING BASIC SERVICES SUCH AS DRINKING WATER
But community leaders in BP's Pedernales area say they lack basic services such as schools, doctors and drinking water, and if an oil company can provide them, so be it.
"Here we have all the problems in the world. Education, zero; health, zero. But the most serious problem of all is (drinking) water," said local councillor Yoannis Martinez.

One reason for the delta's neglect has been its remoteness; there is one road to the state capital Tucupita and the other 16,000 square miles (42,000 sq km) is a maze of river channels, mangrove swamps and islands. The state health authority got its first boat only this month.

In addition to paying $900,000 in taxes to Pedernales municipality last year, BP built a water treatment plant and pipeline, repaired or bought five electricity generators and revived the local hospital, company spokesman Ramon Sosa said.
But not everyone is seeing the benefits.

Of the municipality's 6,000 inhabitants, 75 percent are Warao, but not a single Indian sits on the council and even the director of indigenous affairs is a mixed-race "criollo." Very little of the council's $2 million revenues last year trickled down to the isolated Indian villages of the delta.

"The criollos are becoming more capable of acquiring benefits, while the Warao is being marginalised even more than they were already," Dinan said. "If apertura means anything in this zone, it is the seductive possibility that the Warao community could benefit a great deal."
Martinez, a criollo, said the social problems caused by BP's arrival were outweighed by the benefits and he had not noticed lasting environmental damage.
BENEFITS ALONG WITH THE PROBLEMS

"The company brought a lot of strangers to the community, which created some problems, but BP also brought jobs and benefits," he said. "We managed to elevate this area to the status of a municipality and this enabled us to obtain funds to solve the most pressing problems."

BP has treated more than 2,000 people for diseases, donated school materials and launched a study into the Warao. In a country where 80 percent of the people live in poverty despite daily oil revenues of $45 million, BP is also funding a School of Neighbours to advise the inexperienced municipality on how to manage a budget and provide proper public services.
But the Warao feel left out.

"When the company gives to the mayor and it doesn't get to the Waraos, the Waraos go against the company and the mayor," said Warao leader Simon Zabaleta. "There seems to be interests at work so the Indians abandon the place, so when the oil companies arrive they find an uninhabited zone."
Another Warao spokesman, Celedonio Alcantara, thought the oil companies' seismic work involving explosives was slowly poisoning the fish, their principal source of livelihood.

Zabaleta said among the Warao who want the oil companies to leave are those who believe oil is the "blood of the earth," without which crops will not grow. But he thought the companies could have their uses too.

"They should be orientating the company's social programme towards the indigenous people to build houses, schools, dispensaries," he said, adding that they could even provide outboard motors to the Warao who spend long hours paddling up and down the delta.

"If the government does not extend resources to the indigenous community it gives the drug traffickers the chance to help the Waraos," Zabaleta said, noting that traffickers were a rival source of income in the delta.

Over the centuries, the Warao have seen countless invasions of their home by explorers, missionaries, criollo settlers, drug runners and oil companies. "This might be a level of colonisation that brings something that the others didn't, and that is immense wealth," Dinan said of the latest.
